fatal_errors: The hypothesis assumes a powder-metallurgy/HIP-produced, homogeneous single-phase alloy, whereas the studied material was an arc-melted as-cast alloy with two segregated BCC phases and W-Ta-rich dendritic versus Zr-Ti-rich interdendritic regions.
The proposed 900–1200 °C tensile and fracture tests do not reconstruct the reported room-temperature compression, room-to-500 °C indentation, and room-temperature scratch measurements.

The mechanism assigns improved ductility to lattice distortion lowering the dislocation-glide barrier, while the paper associated lattice distortion and W/Ta frictional resistance primarily with strengthening and tentatively associated damage tolerance with Ti, V, and Zr-related electronic, dislocation-core, grain-boundary, and crack-arrest effects.
No cited prior evidence supports the proposed causal mechanism.
The pure-tungsten baseline is incorrectly described as recrystallized rather than the commercially sourced, powder-sintered, coarse-grained plate actually tested.
explanation: The response addresses the correct broad comparison and predicts the right qualitative direction—greater plastic strain and toughness and a lower ductile-transition temperature than tungsten. However, it reconstructs neither the material state nor the experiments. It replaces the actual segregated, two-BCC-phase as-cast alloy with a hypothetical homogeneous single phase and moves the testing range far beyond the reported room-temperature-to-500 °C regime. Its central causal claim is also poorly aligned with the paper: lattice distortion was invoked mainly for high strength, not demonstrated to lower the Peierls barrier and produce toughness. The proposed matched-processing/TEM study could test this alternative mechanism to some extent, but changing composition simultaneously changes chemistry, phase constitution, segregation, and bonding, so it would not cleanly isolate lattice distortion without additional controls. The falsification rule is testable but bundles several outcomes and lacks supporting evidence.
